---
title: "Coming from ggplot2"
description: >
  A translation guide for ggplot2 users: the same plots built both ways,
  side by side, and the handful of concepts that differ.
---

```{r}
#| include: false
have_all <- all(vapply(
  c("vellum", "vellumplot", "vellumwidget"),
  requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE
))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%",
  eval = have_all
)
if (have_all) suppressMessages(library(vellumverse))
```

If you already think in `ggplot2`, `vellumplot` will feel familiar: data in,
aesthetics mapped to marks, scales and facets and themes layered on top. The
grammar is the same idea. Four things are different, and once they click the
rest is a matter of renaming.

Throughout, the `ggplot2` code is shown for reference and the `vellumplot`
equivalent is the one rendered.

## The four differences

**1. `|>`, not `+`.** Layers are joined with the base pipe. A `vellumplot` plot is
an ordinary pipeline, so the first argument of every verb is the plot.

**2. No `aes()`.** Aesthetics are named arguments on the mark itself. A bare
column name is mapped to data; a single value, literal or held in a variable
that is not a column, is a setting. `color = hp` is a channel with a legend; `color = "red"` paints
everything red. `I()` forces a setting and `.env$x` a mapping.

**3. `geom_*` becomes `mark_*`.** Same layers, different prefix.
`geom_point()` is `mark_point()`, `geom_smooth()` is `mark_smooth()`, and so
on.

**4. A plot is a spec, not a picture.** `vellumplot` builds an inspectable
specification and compiles it only when printed, saved, or made interactive.
`summary()` shows you the spec without drawing it.

## Translation table

| ggplot2 | vellumplot |
|---|---|
| `ggplot(df, aes(x, y))` | `vplot(df)` then `mark_*(x = x, y = y)` |
| `aes(color = z)` | `color = z` on the mark |
| `+` | <code>&#124;&gt;</code> |
| `geom_point()` | `mark_point()` |
| `geom_line()` / `geom_path()` | `mark_line()` / `mark_path()` |
| `geom_col()` / `geom_bar()` | `mark_bar()` |
| `geom_smooth()` | `mark_smooth()` |
| `geom_histogram()` | `mark_histogram()` |
| `geom_boxplot()` | `mark_boxplot()` |
| `geom_tile()` / `geom_raster()` | `mark_tile()` / `mark_raster()` |
| `geom_hex()` | `mark_hex()` |
| `geom_sf()` | `mark_sf()` |
| `geom_hline(yintercept = 0)` / `geom_vline(xintercept = 0)` | `mark_rule(y = 0)` / `mark_rule(x = 0)` |
| `scale_color_continuous()` | `scale_color_continuous()` |
| `scale_*_manual(values = )` | `scale_*_manual(values = )` |
| `facet_wrap(~z)` | `facet_wrap(~z)` |
| `facet_grid(a ~ b)` | `facet_grid(a ~ b)` |
| `facet_wrap(~z, labeller = label_both)` | `facet_wrap(~z, labeller = label_both)` |
| `labeller = label_parsed` / `label_wrap_gen(20)` | `labeller = label_parsed` / `label_wrap_gen(20)` |
| `guides(x = guide_axis(angle = 45))` | `guides(x = guide_axis(angle = 45))` |
| `labs(x = expression(alpha^2))` | `labs(x = expression(alpha^2))`, `plotmath("alpha^2")`, or TeX with `tex()` |
| `geom_text(parse = TRUE)` | `mark_text(parse = TRUE)` |
| `coord_flip()` / `coord_polar()` | `coord_flip()` / `coord_polar()` |
| `theme_minimal()` | `theme_minimal()` |
| `element_text(face = "bold")` | `element_text(face = "bold")`, or a numeric `weight = 600` |
| `theme(strip.clip = "off")` | `theme(strip.clip = "off")` |
| `labs(title = )` | `labs(title = )` |
| `ggsave("p.png")` | `render_plot(p, "p.png")` (also `.svg`, `.pdf`, `.pptx`) |

`labs()` typesets an `expression()` (or a quoted call) as plotmath, as in
`ggplot2`. `plotmath()` takes the same markup as a string, and TeX goes in
`tex()` or between `$...$` inside `md()`.

Note that spelling: `vellumplot` uses American `color` as the primary aesthetic
name (with `colour`/`fill` accepted where it makes sense).

Animation (`gganimate`) and composition (`patchwork`) are built in:

| gganimate / patchwork | vellumplot |
|---|---|
| `+ transition_states(s)` | <code>&#124;&gt; transition_states(s)</code> |
| `+ transition_time(t)` / `+ transition_reveal(t)` | <code>&#124;&gt; transition_time(t)</code> / <code>&#124;&gt; transition_reveal(t)</code> |
| `+ ease_aes("cubic-in-out")` | <code>&#124;&gt; ease_aes(&quot;cubic-in-out&quot;)</code> |
| `animate(p, nframes = 100)` | `animate(p, nframes = 100)` |
| `anim_save("a.gif", a)` | `anim_save("a.gif", a)` (also `.png`/`.apng`, `.svg`) |
| <code>p1 &#124; p2</code> | `hconcat(p1, p2)` |
| `p1 / p2` | `vconcat(p1, p2)` |
| `p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1))` | `vconcat(p1, p2, heights = c(2, 1))` |
| <code>(p1 &#124; p2) + plot_layout(widths = c(2, 1))</code> | `hconcat(p1, p2, widths = c(2, 1))` |
| `wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 2)` | `wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 2)` |
| `p + inset_element(p2, 0.6, 0.6, 1, 1, align_to = "panel")` | `inset(p, p2, 0.6, 0.6, 1, 1, align_to = "panel")` |
| `+ plot_annotation(title = , tag_levels = "A")` | <code>&#124;&gt; compose_annotation(title = , tag_levels = &quot;A&quot;)</code> |

Plots don't combine with `|` and `/`; call the functions. See
[combining plots](#combining-plots) below for an example.

## Scatter with a colour scale

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```r
# ggplot2
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, color = hp)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_continuous()
```

```r
# vellumplot
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  scale_color_continuous()
```
:::

```{r scatter}
#| echo: false
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  scale_color_continuous()
```

## Points with a fitted line

The layering translates one-to-one; the `+` becomes a `|>` and each geom
becomes a mark. Note that `vellumplot` marks carry their own encodings rather than
inheriting a top-level `aes()`.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```r
# ggplot2
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

```r
# vellumplot
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  mark_smooth(x = wt, y = mpg, method = "lm")
```
:::

```{r smooth}
#| echo: false
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  mark_smooth(x = wt, y = mpg, method = "lm")
```

## Faceting

`facet_wrap()` and `facet_grid()` keep their names and their formula
interface.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```r
# ggplot2
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```r
# vellumplot
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl) |>
  theme_minimal()
```
:::

```{r facet}
#| echo: false
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl) |>
  theme_minimal()
```

## A bar chart with a manual palette

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```r
# ggplot2
ggplot(mpg, aes(class, fill = class)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#6b4f2c", "#8a7350")) +
  coord_flip()
```

```r
# vellumplot
vplot(mpg) |>
  mark_bar(x = class, fill = class) |>
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#6b4f2c", "#8a7350")) |>
  coord_flip()
```
:::

## Combining plots

`vconcat()` stacks plots and `heights` sets their share of the figure, as
`plot_layout(heights = )` does in `patchwork`. `compose_annotation()` adds a
figure title and panel tags. Both cells map `color` to `factor(cyl)`, so
their legends are collected into one. The top cell is faceted, so the cells
can't share one panel grid and each is laid out on its own; the title, tags
and collected legend are still drawn around the whole figure.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
```r
# ggplot2 + patchwork
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~am)
p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(hp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point()
p1 / p2 +
  plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1), guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(title = "Weight, mileage and cylinders",
                  tag_levels = "A")
```

```r
# vellumplot
p1 <- vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  facet_wrap(~am)
p2 <- vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = hp, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))
vconcat(p1, p2, heights = c(2, 1)) |>
  compose_annotation(title = "Weight, mileage and cylinders",
                     tag_levels = "A")
```
:::

```{r compose}
#| echo: false
p1 <- vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl)) |>
  facet_wrap(~am)
p2 <- vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = hp, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))
vconcat(p1, p2, heights = c(2, 1)) |>
  compose_annotation(title = "Weight, mileage and cylinders",
                     tag_levels = "A")
```

## What you gain

Two things fall out of the spec-first design.

**Inspect a plot before drawing it.** Because the plot is data, `summary()`
prints its structure. `ggplot2` has a `summary()` method as well, so the
difference is not the function but how far it goes: because `vellum` measures
text and solves layout without a device, the compiled spec can also report where
every element lands before anything renders.

```{r}
#| eval: false
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  summary()
#> <PlotSpec> 32x11 (11 columns), page 6x4 in
#>
#> ── layers
#> • mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp)
```

**Make it interactive without a second plot.** The same spec, handed to
`as_widget()`, becomes an HTML widget, and the interactive channels (`tooltip`,
`data_id`) are just more mark arguments. `ggiraph` and `plotly` get you to a
client-side widget from `ggplot2` too; the difference is that there are no
`*_interactive()` twins of the marks to swap in, and the widget renders the same
compiled scene as the static figure rather than redrawing the plot in another
engine:

```{r}
#| eval: false
df <- data.frame(wt = mtcars$wt, mpg = mtcars$mpg, model = rownames(mtcars))

vplot(df) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, tooltip = model, data_id = model) |>
  as_widget()
```

## What is different by design

A few `ggplot2` habits do not carry over, on purpose:

- There is no global `aes()` shared across layers; each mark states its own
  encodings. This is more verbose for multi-layer plots but removes the
  inheritance rules you have to keep in your head.
- `+` chaining and its operator methods are gone; everything is a function
  in a pipe.
- Saving is `render_plot()`, not `ggsave()`, and one spec renders to PNG,
  SVG, PDF, and an editable PowerPoint slide (`.pptx`) from the same object.
  See [one scene, many outputs](one-scene-many-outputs.html).
- Rows with a missing position or size are dropped with one "Removed n rows
  containing missing values" warning per layer, as in `ggplot2`, and a
  continuous size legend shows no "NA" key. An area or ribbon leaves a gap at
  a missing value and counts it in that warning. A line also breaks at a
  missing value rather than joining across it, but doesn't count it in the
  warning yet.

For the exhaustive list of marks, scales, coords, and themes, see the
[vellumplot reference](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellumplot/).
